content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published consolidated guidelines on the treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB), which include evidence-based recommendations for managing multidrug-resistant and rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB). These guidelines, updated in 2019, replace previous WHO recommendations issued since 2011 and provide comprehensive guidance on treatment regimens, patient care, and monitoring. The guidelines allow for the reproduction, adaptation, and redistribution of the content for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. However, the WHO logo cannot be used, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or equivalent Creative Commons license. Translations must include a disclaimer stating that WHO is not responsible for the accuracy or content of the translation, and the original English version remains the authoritative source. The guidelines emphasize that WHO does not endorse specific organizations, products, or services, and any disputes arising from the use of the material must follow the mediation rules of the World Intellectual Property Organization. Users are responsible for obtaining permission to reuse third-party materials and bear the risk of any claims related to copyright infringement. The document includes detailed recommendations for the treatment of isoniazid-resistant TB (Hr-TB) and MDR/RR-TB, including the use of longer and shorter treatment regimens, culture monitoring, timing of antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV-infected patients, surgical interventions, and patient support models. The guidelines also provide definitions of key terms, such as drug-susceptibility testing (DST), intensive treatment phases, and classifications of drug resistance. For isoniazid-resistant TB, a six-month regimen of rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, and levofloxacin is recommended. Injectable agents like streptomycin are not advised for these patients. For MDR/RR-TB, longer regimens lasting 18–20 months are suggested, with modifications based on the patient’s response to therapy. Shorter regimens of 9–12 months may be used in specific cases where resistance to fluoroquinolones and second-line injectable agents has been excluded. The guidelines recommend the inclusion of specific drugs in MDR/RR-TB regimens, such as bedaquiline, linezolid, clofazimine, and cycloserine, while avoiding kanamycin and capreomycin. Delamanid may be included for patients aged three years or older. Monitoring treatment response involves monthly sputum culture testing in addition to smear microscopy. ART should be initiated as early as possible (within eight weeks) for all HIV-infected patients requiring second-line TB treatment. Elective partial lung resection surgery may be considered for MDR/RR-TB patients as part of their treatment plan. Patient care and support are critical components of the guidelines. Health education, counseling, and adherence support should be provided, with options such as directly observed treatment (DOT), video-observed treatment (VOT), and unsupervised treatment tailored to individual needs. Ambulatory care is preferred over hospitalization, and decentralized care models are recommended. The guidelines also address the importance of psychological and material support, such as counseling, peer-group support, food assistance, and financial subsidies, to mitigate the indirect costs and income loss associated with TB treatment. These consolidated guidelines aim to improve the treatment and care of patients with drug-resistant TB, aligning with WHO’s End TB Strategy and global health goals.
